# The Rocky Mountain News Prints Its Final Edition

**(CNN)** After nearly 150 years of continuous publication, the *Rocky Mountain News* released its final edition on Friday—another casualty of a faltering economy and the rise of digital media. The Denver-based newspaper's closing front-page headline read simply: "Goodbye, Colorado."

"It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today," the paper wrote. "Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over."

The announcement came from the paper's owner, E.W. Scripps Co., delivered to the newsroom at noon on Thursday and bringing to an end three months of speculation surrounding the publication's fate since it was put up for sale in December.

The *Rocky Mountain News* joins a growing list of casualties in an industry beset by closures, layoffs, and austerity measures. "It's in a free fall, and nobody knows where the bottom is," said media critic Eric Alterman. "It's kind of like water in the toilet swirling around, and nobody knows what's left when you're done flushing."

**Watch how the economy and the Internet are reshaping the industry »**

Newspapers nationwide are grappling with declining readership and advertising revenue as more Americans turn to the internet for news. "All newspapers are under great pressure," said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the *New York Daily News*—the seventh-largest paper in the country by circulation. "They'll survive, but in different forms. Their cost base will have to be dramatically lowered."

The steep decline in advertising revenue amid a punishing economy has forced newspapers to slash costs—often through layoffs of cartoonists, columnists, and other staff—leaving many to seek new careers in a struggling field. Pia Catton lost her position as arts editor at the *New York Sun* five months ago when the paper folded. Though she has since taken on a short-term book-editing project, she suspects she may soon need to consider a different career path altogether. "There will always be a market for news—you will always need to know immediately what's happening," she said. "Will there be a market for newspapers? That's another question."

According to the Columbia Journalism Review's website, the *Rocky Mountain News* employed more than 200 editorial staff members. Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, told employees that the closure stemmed from a punishing economy, sweeping upheaval within the newspaper industry, and multimillion-dollar annual losses. "Denver can't support two newspapers any longer," Boehne said. "It's certainly not good news for you, and it's certainly not good news for Denver."

Since 2001, the *News* had operated under a joint operating agreement with *The Denver Post*, merging the two papers' business functions to cut costs while keeping their editorial staffs separate. With the *News*'s closure, Denver now joins the ranks of most American cities served by a single major newspaper.

"We've been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long," said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor at the paper. "What a huge loss for Colorado today."

The news comes amid broader turmoil in the industry: this week, the *San Francisco Chronicle* announced it, too, risks closure or sale unless it can stem its financial losses. Officials from the Hearst Corporation, which owns the *Chronicle*, revealed the paper lost $50 million in 2008 and is on track to lose even more this year.

"It's difficult. It's hard," said Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year veteran of Scripps, reflecting on the closure. "I haven't returned any phone calls yet, because I don't need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I've done enough of that already."

Video footage posted on the paper's website captured a newsroom filled with somber faces—and, occasionally, quiet sobs—as the weight of the closure settled in among staff. "I could say stupid things like 'I know how you feel.' I don't," Boehne told employees. "We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that."

*CNN's Richard Roth contributed to this report.*

# Denver's Historic Newspaper Prints Its Final Pages

(CNN) -- Following a run of almost 150 years, the Rocky Mountain News released its concluding edition on Friday, succumbing to economic hardship and the rise of digital media. This Denver, Colorado publication closed its doors after a century and a half of operation. Its concluding front page carried a simple, poignant message: "Goodbye, Colorado." The farewell statement read: "It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over."

E.W. Scripps Co., the paper's parent company, delivered the news to staff members during a Thursday noon meeting, finally resolving months of uncertainty that had gripped the organization since December, when the paper was first listed for sale.

This closure represents merely the newest casualty in a wave of industry-wide shutdowns, staff reductions, and budget slashing sweeping through American journalism. Media analyst Eric Alterman described the situation starkly: "It's in a free fall and nobody knows where the bottom is. It's kind of like water in the toilet swirling around and nobody knows what's left when you're done flushing."

## An Industry in Crisis

Publications nationwide face mounting challenges as subscriber numbers dwindle and advertisers pull back, with consumers increasingly turning to internet sources for their news. Mort Zuckerman, who publishes the New York Daily News—currently ranked seventh in national circulation—offered his perspective: "All newspapers are under great pressure. They'll survive, but they'll survive in different forms, their costs base will have to be dramatically lowered."

This severe drop in advertising income during tough economic times has pushed papers to slash expenses through layoffs affecting cartoonists, columnists, and countless other staff members, who now find themselves navigating an uncertain job market. Pia Catton experienced this firsthand when she lost her position as arts editor at the New York Sun five months prior to that paper's closure. Though she's found temporary work editing a manuscript, she anticipates needing to explore entirely different career paths. "There will always be a market for news, you will always need to know immediately what's happening," she noted. "Will there be a market for newspapers? That's another question."

## The End of an Era in Denver

According to the Columbia Journalism Review's website, the Rocky Mountain News employed over 200 people in its editorial department. Scripps CEO Rich Boehne explained to staff that the combination of a devastating economic climate, industry-wide turmoil, and years of substantial financial losses sealed the paper's fate. "Denver can't support two newspapers any longer," he stated bluntly. "It's certainly not good news for you, and it's certainly not good news for Denver."

Since 2001, the News had operated under a joint business arrangement with the Denver Post, merging their commercial operations to cut expenses while maintaining separate news departments. With this shutdown, Denver joins the ranks of most American cities that now support only a single major newspaper. Presentation editor Mel Pompanio reflected on the paper's precarious position: "We've been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long. What a huge loss for Colorado today."

## Ripple Effects Across the Industry

Adding to industry anxieties, the San Francisco Chronicle revealed this same week that it faces potential sale or closure unless its financial losses can be stemmed. Representatives from Hearst Corp., which owns the Chronicle, reported the paper hemorrhaged $50 million in 2008, with even steeper losses projected for the current year.

Lynn Bartels, a 26-year Scripps veteran working as a political reporter, struggled to process the closure announcement: "It's difficult. It's hard. I haven't returned any phone calls yet, because I don't need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I've done that enough."

Footage posted to the newspaper's website captured the somber mood in the newsroom, where staff members' expressions reflected the gravity of the moment, punctuated by audible sobs as the reality of the closure set in. Boehne acknowledged the emotional weight of the situation: "I could say stupid things like 'I know how you feel.' I don't. We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that."

*CNN's Richard Roth contributed to this report.*

# The Rocky Mountain News Closes: A Newspaper Industry in Crisis

After serving the Denver community for an astonishing 150 years, the Rocky Mountain News published its final edition, marking the end of an era for one of America's oldest newspapers. The closure sent shockwaves through the journalism community, not because it was unprecedented, but precisely because it wasn't—it represented the latest in a growing list of newspaper casualties across the United States, each one underscoring the severity of a crisis that has been building for years.

The forces behind the Rocky Mountain News's demise are the same ones plaguing newspapers nationwide. Readership has been steadily declining as audiences shift away from traditional print media. Advertising revenue, once the lifeblood of newspaper operations, has dried up as businesses redirect their marketing budgets toward digital platforms that offer more targeted and cost-effective reach. Perhaps most significantly, the rise of internet news consumption has fundamentally altered how people access information, with readers increasingly turning to websites, blogs, and social media for their news rather than waiting for the morning paper.

This confluence of factors has created what industry experts describe as a "free fall"—a term that captures both the severity and unpredictability of the crisis. Unlike previous downturns in the newspaper business, this one shows no signs of stabilizing. Newspapers across the country have responded with drastic measures: widespread layoffs have become commonplace, newsrooms have been gutted, physical page counts have shrunk, and some publications have reduced their printing schedules or moved to online-only formats in desperate attempts to cut costs and remain viable.

Media analysts and industry veterans have struggled to predict where this trajectory will lead. The traditional business model that sustained newspapers for generations—one built on print advertising and subscription revenue—appears fundamentally broken, and no clear replacement has emerged to take its place. Some newspapers have experimented with paywalls, digital subscriptions, and nonprofit funding models, but these alternatives have yet to prove they can fully replace the lost revenue streams.

The loss of the Rocky Mountain News represents more than just the disappearance of a media outlet; it symbolizes the erosion of local journalism and the diminishing number of reporters covering community news, government accountability, and regional issues. As more newspapers face similar fates, questions loom about the future of print journalism in America and what will fill the void left behind—both in terms of information access and the watchdog role newspapers have historically played in a democratic society. With no end to the "free fall" in sight, the industry finds itself at a critical crossroads, uncertain of what comes next.

**Rocky Mountain News Publishes Final Edition, Ending 150-Year Run**

DENVER — The Rocky Mountain News, one of the oldest newspapers in the American West, published its final edition Friday, closing the book on a publication that had chronicled life in Colorado since before the state itself existed.

E.W. Scripps Company, the paper's owner, announced this week that it could not find a buyer willing to keep the News operating, citing a steep decline in advertising revenue and the broader economic pressures battering the newspaper industry. The closure puts roughly 230 employees out of work.

"Nobody wanted this to happen," said John Temple, the paper's editor, president and publisher, who choked back tears while addressing the staff. "This is a business decision in the face of a broken business model."

Founded in 1859, just weeks after gold was discovered in the region, the Rocky Mountain News predated Colorado's admission to the union by 17 years. Over the course of a century and a half, it covered the Gold Rush, two world wars, the Columbine High School shooting, and countless other stories that shaped the identity of Denver and the Mountain West.

The paper won four Pulitzer Prizes, including one in 2000 for its coverage of the Columbine massacre and another in 2003 for photography documenting Colorado's devastating wildfires.

Scripps had owned the News since 1926. In recent years it operated under a joint agency agreement with MediaNews Group's Denver Post, sharing business operations while maintaining separate newsrooms — an arrangement increasingly common among struggling metro dailies. But that partnership wasn't enough to offset the paper's losses, which Scripps said topped $16 million last year alone.

The News is among a growing list of American newspapers to shut down, cut staff, or seek bankruptcy protection amid the migration of readers and advertisers to the internet. The Seattle Post-Intelligencer has warned it may stop print publication in the coming weeks, and papers in cities including Philadelphia, Minneapolis, and San Diego's Tribune Publishing have filed for bankruptcy protection in recent months.

Friday's final edition ran under the headline "Goodbye, Colorado," with the front page featuring a photo collage spanning the paper's history. Inside, staffers reflected on the paper's legacy and thanked readers for a century and a half of loyalty.

Reporters and editors described a newsroom thick with grief but also pride, as colleagues embraced and swapped stories about the assignments and front pages they wouldn't forget.

"We didn't lose. We were just failed by a business model that was failing all around the country," Temple told staff. "Everybody in this room should hold your heads high."

The Denver Post will continue publishing as the city's sole major daily newspaper.

# Rocky Mountain News Ceases Publication After 150 Years

**DENVER** — The Rocky Mountain News, Colorado's oldest newspaper, published its final edition, becoming one of the most prominent casualties in an industry facing unprecedented economic upheaval.

The E.W. Scripps Co., which owned the paper, announced it could not find a buyer willing to continue operating the 150-year-old publication, which had been losing money for years despite maintaining a loyal readership base.

## A Familiar Story Across the Industry

The Rocky Mountain News' demise reflects broader challenges plaguing newspapers nationwide. Circulation revenue has declined for years, but the more devastating blow has come from the collapse of advertising revenue—particularly classified ads, which migrated to free online platforms like Craigslist. Display advertising has also suffered as businesses shift marketing budgets toward digital channels.

The recession compounded these structural problems, as retailers, auto dealers, and real estate companies—traditionally major newspaper advertisers—slashed their marketing spending amid economic uncertainty.

Denver's situation was particularly precarious because it was one of the few remaining American cities with two competing daily newspapers. The Rocky Mountain News and the Denver Post had operated under a joint operating agreement, sharing business and printing operations while maintaining separate newsrooms—an arrangement increasingly untenable as the overall market for print advertising shrank.

## Not an Isolated Case

The Rocky Mountain News' closure came amid warnings about the fate of other major metropolitan newspapers. The San Francisco Chronicle, owned by Hearst Corporation, faced similar existential threats, with the company publicly stating it would shut down the paper unless significant cost reductions—including potential staff cuts and union concessions—could be achieved quickly.

Other newspapers around the country announced bankruptcy filings, ownership changes, reduced print schedules, or moves to online-only formats. The Tribune Company, owner of the Chicago Tribune and Los Angeles Times, had already filed for bankruptcy protection months earlier.

## Industry-Wide Reckoning

Media analysts pointed to several converging factors accelerating the crisis:

- **Digital disruption**: Readers increasingly turned to free online news sources, undermining subscription and single-copy sales
- **Advertising migration**: Online competitors captured advertising dollars once exclusive to print
- **Debt burdens**: Many newspaper chains had taken on significant debt during acquisitions in more prosperous times, leaving them vulnerable when revenues declined
- **Changing consumption habits**: Younger readers showed diminishing interest in traditional print subscriptions

## Human and Civic Cost

Beyond the immediate loss of roughly 200 jobs, media observers expressed concern about the broader implications for civic journalism. Newspapers have historically provided in-depth local reporting, investigative journalism, and accountability coverage of local government and institutions—functions that many worried would not be adequately replaced by emerging digital-only outlets.

The closure prompted renewed debate about sustainable business models for journalism, with some advocating for nonprofit ownership structures, reader-funded models, or new digital subscription approaches as potential paths forward for an industry in profound transition.

---

*This piece reflects the media landscape and economic conditions of early 2009, a period of severe crisis for American newspapers.*

# End of an Era: The Herald-Tribune Closes Its Doors After 127 Years

The presses fell silent for the last time Thursday at the Herald-Tribune, marking the end of a publication that had chronicled the life of this city since 1897. The closure, announced three weeks ago, has left 214 employees without jobs and residents mourning the loss of an institution many considered as permanent as the courthouse it once stood beside.

## A Perfect Storm

Newspaper executives pointed to a combination of factors that made the closure inevitable: a advertising revenue collapse tied to the broader economic downturn, coupled with an irreversible shift of readers toward digital news sources.

"We fought this for over a decade," said publisher Margaret Chen, who joined the paper in 2019 hoping to reverse its fortunes. "We tried paywalls, we tried free digital models, we tried cutting the print schedule to three days a week. But when advertising revenue drops by 60 percent in five years and your primary competitors are Google and Facebook rather than other newspapers, there's only so much restructuring can accomplish."

Chen said the recession proved to be the final blow to a business model already weakened by years of digital disruption. "Local businesses that used to buy full-page ads simply stopped advertising altogether during the downturn. They didn't move that money to our website—they cut it entirely or shifted to social media platforms where they could reach customers for free."

## Voices from the Newsroom

For staff members, many of whom had spent decades at the paper, the closure represents both a personal and professional loss.

Investigative reporter David Ostrowski, who spent 23 years at the Herald-Tribune, described the newsroom's final days as somber but proud.

"We broke stories that changed this city," Ostrowski said, gesturing to a wall of framed front pages being carefully packed into boxes. "The water contamination story, the school board corruption case—that's not something you get from a Twitter feed. That takes time, resources, and institutional knowledge that took years to build."

Photojournalist Elena Vasquez, who started as an intern in 2015, expressed frustration about the broader industry trends that led to this moment.

"People want news for free, and they want it instantly, but they don't think about what's lost when there's no one left to actually go to the city council meeting, or file the public records request, or spend six months investigating a story," Vasquez said. "I don't know where accountability journalism goes from here in this city."

Copy editor Frank Delgado, 61, who had worked at the paper since 1987, struggled to articulate what the loss meant to him.

"This was my career, my community, my identity in some ways," Delgado said. "I'm 61 years old. I'm not sure who's hiring copy editors right now, especially in print media. But more than that—I keep thinking about all the readers who relied on us. The elderly folks who don't use computers. Who tells them what's happening in their town now?"

## The Numbers Behind the Closure

Financial documents released by the company show the stark reality facing the Herald-Tribune. Print circulation had fallen from 145,000 daily readers in 2005 to just 22,000 by this year. Digital subscriptions, despite aggressive marketing campaigns, never exceeded 8,000 paying subscribers—far short of the 25,000 that executives had projected would be necessary for sustainability.

Advertising revenue, once the paper's primary income source, dropped from $34 million annually in 2007 to under $4 million this year.

"The math simply stopped working," said Chief Financial Officer Robert Yamamoto. "We were spending more to produce quality journalism than we could generate in revenue, regardless of platform. This isn't unique to us—it's happening to newspapers across the country, but that doesn't make it any less painful."

## A Community Responds

News of the closure prompted an outpouring of reaction from readers and community leaders. City Council member Patricia Holbrook called the closure "a genuine loss for democracy at the local level."

"Who's going to cover the zoning board meetings now? The school budget hearings?" Holbrook asked. "These aren't glamorous stories, but they're the stories that keep local government honest. I worry about what happens in the vacuum."

Local resident Margaret Sinclair, 78, said she had subscribed to the paper for over 50 years. "I read it every morning with my coffee. It's not just news—it was a ritual, a connection to this community. I don't know what I'll do now. My daughter keeps telling me to get a tablet, but that's not the same thing."

## What Comes Next

Chen said a skeleton crew of six employees will maintain a limited digital presence, focusing primarily on breaking news alerts and aggregating content from other sources, though she acknowledged this represents a fundamentally different mission than the paper's historic role.

"We're not going to pretend this is a continuation of what the Herald-Tribune was," Chen said. "That paper—the one with investigative teams and dedicated beat reporters and a robust editorial board—that paper is gone. What we're left with is a shadow of that legacy, and I think it's important to be honest about that distinction."

As employees left the building for the final time Thursday evening, many paused to take photographs of the now-dark building that had housed the paper since 1962. The presses, which once ran through the night producing tomorrow's edition, sat silent—a mechanical symbol of an industry in irreversible transition.

"I keep thinking about all the papers that came before us that shut down, and how each time, people said the same things we're saying now," Ostrowski reflected. "The difference is, this time, there's no clear answer for what replaces us. That's what keeps me up at night—not losing my job, but wondering who's going to hold power accountable in this town."

# Rocky Mountain News Prints Final Edition, Ending 150-Year Run

**DENVER** — The presses fell silent this week at the Rocky Mountain News, as Colorado's oldest newspaper published its final edition after 150 years of continuous operation, becoming one of the most prominent casualties yet in an industry beset by plummeting advertising revenue, mounting debt, and a wrenching shift toward digital media.

The 52-page farewell edition, titled "Goodbye, Colorado," hit newsstands with a print run swollen well beyond normal circulation as collectors and longtime readers scrambled for a keepsake copy of the paper that first began publishing in 1859, predating Colorado's statehood by nearly two decades.

## The End of an Era

E.W. Scripps Company, which had owned the Rocky Mountain News since 1926, announced it would cease publication after failing to find a buyer despite weeks of searching. The company said the paper had lost more than $16 million in 2008 alone, a casualty of the same forces battering newspapers nationwide: a historic collapse in classified and display advertising, declining print circulation, and the recession's brutal squeeze on already-thin margins.

"This is the saddest day of my professional life," said John Temple, the paper's editor, president, and publisher, addressing a newsroom of stunned staffers. Many employees learned of the closure only hours before it was made public, gathering in the newsroom to absorb the news together rather than through a press release.

Roughly 220 employees lost their jobs in the closure — reporters, photographers, editors, and support staff, some of whom had spent decades chronicling the life of the Rocky Mountain state.

## A Newspaper's Legacy

Throughout its history, the Rocky Mountain News built a reputation for aggressive local journalism, winning four Pulitzer Prizes, including one in 2000 for its coverage of the Columbine High School massacre and another in 2003 for photography documenting Colorado's devastating wildfires. It had long been locked in a fierce rivalry with the Denver Post, a competition that defined the city's media landscape for generations.

That rivalry had already been curtailed in 2001, when the two papers entered into a joint operating agreement, sharing printing and business operations while maintaining separate newsrooms — a arrangement increasingly common among American newspapers seeking to survive shrinking revenues. With the Rocky's closure, Denver becomes a one-newspaper town, joining a growing list of American cities losing the built-in accountability and competition that comes with multiple daily papers.

## An Industry in Crisis

The Rocky Mountain News's demise is emblematic of a broader reckoning within the newspaper industry. Papers across the country have slashed staff, reduced print schedules, or shuttered entirely as the internet siphons away both readers and advertisers who once relied on newspapers for classifieds, real estate listings, and job postings — revenue streams that migrated to websites like Craigslist, Monster.com, and countless online competitors.

Media analysts have pointed to several converging pressures: the 2008 financial crisis, which gutted already-weakened ad budgets; enormous debt loads carried by newspaper chains from earlier acquisitions; and a fundamental, seemingly irreversible shift in how Americans consume news. The Tribune Company, owner of the Los Angeles Times and Chicago Tribune, had filed for bankruptcy protection just months earlier. Other major papers, including the San Francisco Chronicle, were reportedly facing existential threats of their own.

"What's happening in Denver is a preview of what we're going to see in city after city," said one media industry analyst. "The economics of print journalism, particularly for second papers in joint operating agreements, have simply collapsed. Advertisers have more options, readers have more options, and the traditional subscription-and-ad model that sustained newspapers for a century no longer works."

Analysts noted that while online readership for many newspapers has grown substantially, digital advertising revenue has not come close to replacing what's been lost in print — a gap that has left news organizations searching, largely in vain, for a sustainable business model.

## Staff Reflect on Loss

For many at the Rocky Mountain News, the closure was felt as a deeply personal loss, not just a business story.

"You spend your whole career building something, telling people's stories, holding this state accountable, and then it just ends," said one longtime staffer, echoing a sentiment expressed throughout the newsroom in the paper's final days. Some employees produced a poignant behind-the-scenes video documenting their final hours in the building, capturing tears, embraces, and the surreal experience of putting out one last edition even as they processed the loss of their jobs.

The final front page featured a photo collage of images from the paper's history alongside the simple, elegiac headline marking its closure — a front page many staffers described as both a tribute and an obituary.

## What Comes Next

Media experts say the Rocky Mountain News's closure raises urgent questions about the future of local journalism and civic accountability in mid-sized American cities. With fewer competing news organizations, some worry that government and corporate accountability will suffer, as fewer journalists remain to cover statehouses, city councils, courts, and communities.

Denver's Rocky Mountain News joins a lengthening list of newspapers that have closed, downsized, or filed for bankruptcy protection amid the industry's turmoil — a trend that shows no sign of abating as the recession deepens and the digital transformation of media continues to accelerate.

For now, Denver readers are left with the Denver Post as their sole daily newspaper, and an industry watching nervously to see which paper might be next.
